title: The Day of Atonement
summary: After the death of Aaron's two sons, God tells Moses how and when Aaron may enter the Most Holy Place: once a year, dressed in plain linen, with blood and a cloud of incense. Aaron purifies the sanctuary with the blood of a bull and a goat, then confesses Israel's sins over a second, living goat and sends it into the wilderness. The day becomes a permanent annual fast and Sabbath for all Israel.
story:
The chapter opens by reaching back to Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire and died before the LORD. That disaster raised the question the whole book has been circling since the glory of the LORD filled the newly finished tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and Moses himself could not enter: how can a holy God live in the middle of a sinful, impure people without consuming them? Chapters 11 to 15 dealt with the uncleanness of daily life, from food to skin disease to bodily discharges, each with its own washing or offering. Chapter 16 gathers up everything those laws could not reach, the impurity and rebellion that build up over a year and cling to the sanctuary itself, and deals with it in one great annual cleansing.

The chapter stands near the center of Leviticus, and it is the hinge between the laws of purity before it and the call to holy living in chapters 17 to 27, which scholars since August Klostermann (1877) have called the Holiness Code. What was lost in Eden, the presence of God among his people, has been restored in the tabernacle; this chapter provides the means by which that presence can remain. Its date, the tenth day of the seventh month, is fixed again in the festival calendar of Leviticus 23:26-32, and the day it establishes, Yom Kippur, is still the holiest day of the Jewish year.
historical:
Leviticus presents these instructions as given at Mount Sinai in the year after the exodus, while Israel camped around the newly built tabernacle, the portable tent-sanctuary described in Exodus 25 to 40. As with the rest of the Pentateuch, the date of writing is debated. Tradition credits the material to Moses. Julius Wellhausen and many who followed him assigned the priestly material, Leviticus 1 to 16 included, to the time of the Babylonian exile or after it, in the sixth or fifth century BC. Yehezkel Kaufmann and Jacob Milgrom argued that the priestly source is older than the exile, and others argue that its rituals fit the world of the second millennium BC. Milgrom also proposed that verses 2 to 28 once described an emergency purification the high priest could perform whenever the sanctuary was defiled, and that verses 29 to 34 later fixed it to one day a year; others read the chapter as a unity from the start.

Israel's neighbors had rites for cleansing temples and carrying evil away. Two ritual texts from Ebla in Syria, from about the twenty-fourth century BC, describe a she-goat with a silver bracelet at its neck being driven out into the wasteland of Alini as part of purification rites for the king's wedding; Ida Zatelli drew attention to them as parallels in 1998. Hittite ritual texts from Anatolia, such as the rituals of Ashella and Uhhamuwa, drive a ram or other animal toward enemy territory to carry a plague away from the army or the land. In the Babylonian New Year festival, on the fifth day of the month Nisan, a priest purified the shrine of the god Nabu by wiping it with the carcass of a slaughtered ram, which was then thrown into the river, and the men who handled it had to stay outside the city until the festival ended. Leviticus 16 shares the basic idea that impurity can be removed physically, but it has no incantations, no demons to appease, and no magic: everything is done because the LORD commanded it, and the goat carries confessed sin, not disease.

The ritual was practiced for centuries in the Second Temple. By then the ark had been lost, and the Mishnah says the high priest sprinkled the blood toward the place where it had stood, over a rock called the foundation stone (m. Yoma 5:2). Philo of Alexandria describes the day as the Fast, observed even by those who kept little else of the law (On the Special Laws 2.193-203), and Josephus summarizes the rite (Antiquities 3.240-243). The Temple Scroll from Qumran gives its own version of the ritual (11QT 25-27), and the Qumran commentary on Habakkuk records that the Wicked Priest pursued the Teacher of Righteousness on the Teacher's Day of Atonement (1QpHab 11:4-8), a sign that the community kept the day on a different calendar from the temple. The book of Acts calls the season simply the Fast (Acts 27:9). The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish legal tradition compiled around AD 200, devotes a whole tractate, Yoma (Aramaic for the Day), to how the day was kept, including the report that by the late Second Temple the goat was led to a ravine in the desert and pushed backward over the edge (m. Yoma 6:6). After the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, the sacrifices ceased, and Jews kept the day through prayer, fasting, confession, and the recital of the high priest's service.
cultural:
For a first reader the tabernacle was a house with rooms of rising holiness: the courtyard with its altar of burnt offering, the Holy Place with its lampstand, table, and incense altar, and behind a thick woven curtain the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant stood and God's presence appeared above its gold lid, the mercy seat, between the two cherubim. Ordinary priests served daily in the Holy Place. No one entered the inner room except the high priest, and only on this day. He did not wear the jeweled breastpiece and gold-trimmed robes of Exodus 28 but a plain linen tunic, undergarments, sash, and turban, more like a servant's dress, and he bathed before putting them on. White linen was also the clothing of heavenly figures in Israel's visions (Ezekiel 9:2, Daniel 10:5). The Mishnah adds that he immersed himself five times during the day (m. Yoma 3:3). The cloud of incense covered the mercy seat so that he would not die.

The chapter assumes that sin and impurity do not stay with the sinner. They pollute the place where God dwells, the way smoke stains a house. Impurity (tum'ah) in Leviticus is not the same as sin: it comes from ordinary events such as childbirth, skin disease, bodily discharges, and contact with death (Leviticus 12 to 15), and it had to be kept apart from the holy. The blood sprinkled on and before the mercy seat, in the tent, and on the altar cleanses those places “because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites” (verse 16), reaching both kinds of defilement, including deliberate rebellion, which the ordinary sin offerings did not cover. Then the second goat deals with the people's guilt itself, carrying it out of the camp into the wilderness, the realm of desolation outside the ordered world of the camp.

The laying on of hands was a familiar gesture from the ordinary offerings (Leviticus 1:4, 4:4), where the worshiper pressed one hand on the animal's head. Here Aaron uses both hands and speaks a confession aloud, which makes the transfer explicit. The instruction that the people “humble yourselves” (verse 29) was understood as fasting (Isaiah 58:3-5, Psalm 35:13), and the day was the only fast required by the law of Moses. The Mishnah lists five abstentions: from eating and drinking, washing, anointing with oil, wearing sandals, and marital relations (m. Yoma 8:1), which remain the customs of Yom Kippur. The command applied to native Israelites and resident foreigners alike, and the day was a Sabbath of complete rest, one of only two days, with the weekly Sabbath, given that title.
literary:
The chapter is a ritual text, written as instruction. It opens with a narrative frame (verses 1-2), lists what Aaron must bring and wear (verses 3-5), gives a quick summary of the rite (verses 6-10), and only then walks through it slowly (verses 11-28). This pattern of summary followed by detailed account is common in ancient ritual texts, and it explains why the bull and the lots are mentioned twice. The detailed account moves outward in space: from the Most Holy Place (verses 11-17), to the altar (verses 18-19), to the head of the live goat and the wilderness beyond the camp (verses 20-22), and back to the tent and the burning outside the camp (verses 23-28). The effect is of holiness restored at the center and defilement carried to the edge.

The verb kipper, to make atonement, occurs sixteen times and binds the whole text together. Its objects widen and narrow: Aaron and his household, the holy place, the tent, the altar, the priests, and all the people. The vocabulary of wrong gathers here as nowhere else in Leviticus: impurities, rebellions, iniquities, and sins (verses 16, 21). The closing paragraph (verses 29-34) turns from the priest to the people and fixes the date, repeating three times that this is “a permanent statute” (verses 29, 31, 34). The chapter ends as it began, with Moses and Aaron and the LORD's command, but the ending reverses the opening: Nadab and Abihu died when they came near in a way the LORD had not commanded, and the final line, “And all this was done as the LORD had commanded Moses”, marks obedience.

outline.t: A warning after the death of Aaron's sons
What Aaron must bring and wear
The bull and the two goats, chosen by lot
Blood inside the veil: cleansing the sanctuary and the altar
The live goat carries the people's sins away
Washing, burnt offerings, and burning outside the camp
A permanent statute for the tenth day of the seventh month

doctrines.note: The chapter shows atonement in two movements: blood that cleanses what sin has defiled, and a goat that carries confessed guilt away. Both are God's provision, not Israel's bargaining; Leviticus 17:11 says God has given the blood for this purpose. The result is stated in verse 30: the people are made clean from all their sins before the LORD.

The sanctuary is where God dwells among his people, and it is described as abiding among them “because it is surrounded by their impurities” (verse 16). Israel's sins do not stay private; they reach the place of God's presence, which must be cleansed if he is to remain. The annual cleansing keeps the dwelling habitable for the holy God.

God's presence is a gift that can kill. Access to him is real but ordered: one man, one day, one room, in the right clothes and with the right blood (verses 2, 34). Holiness here is not fussiness but the reality of who God is, which the death of Aaron's sons (verse 1) made unmistakable.

The text names sin with several words: impurities, rebellious acts, iniquities, and sins (verses 16 and 21). Sin is not only an act that is over once it is done; it leaves a stain on the community and the place of worship that has to be dealt with, and it must be confessed aloud (verse 21).

The high priest acts as Israel's representative before God, first for himself and his household and then for all the people (verses 6, 11, 17, 24). The office passes to each anointed successor (verse 32), a pattern Hebrews 7 to 10 reads as fulfilled in Christ, the priest who needs no offering for himself.

words.note: Kipper, to make atonement. The Piel verb occurs about a hundred times in the Old Testament, nearly half of them in Leviticus, and sixteen times in this chapter. Its meaning is debated. Some link it to covering, others to wiping clean or purging, as with the Akkadian kuppuru used for ritual cleansing, and others to the noun kofer, a ransom price paid to spare a life (Exodus 30:12). In this chapter the objects of the verb include places (the sanctuary, the tent, the altar) as well as people, which suggests cleansing is central. Jay Sklar (Sin, Impurity, Sacrifice, Atonement, 2005) argues that kipper joins both ideas: where sin is in view it means ransom with an element of purging, and where impurity is in view it means purging with an element of ransom.

Kapporet, the mercy seat or atonement cover: the gold lid of the ark, with the two cherubim above it, where God appeared. It occurs 27 times, all in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles 28:11, and seven times in this chapter. The word shares a root with kipper, and the name mercy seat comes from Tyndale, following Luther's Gnadenstuhl. The Septuagint rendered it hilastērion, the word Hebrews 9:5 uses for the mercy seat and Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25, where the BSB has “the atoning sacrifice”.

Azazel, the name given to the second goat's destination, found only in this chapter (verses 8, 10 twice, and 26). Its meaning is disputed. It has been read as a description of the goat itself, the goat that goes away (the Septuagint and Vulgate, and so Tyndale's scapegoat, 1530), as a place name for a rugged cliff in the desert (the Talmud, b. Yoma 67b, and Rashi), as an abstract term for complete removal, or as the name of a wilderness spirit, a reading found in 1 Enoch. On any reading, the goat is not an offering to Azazel; only the LORD receives sacrifice here.

Chatta't, the sin offering. The word occurs nearly three hundred times, meaning both sin and the offering for it, and the offering is named for what it deals with. Jacob Milgrom and others have argued it is better called a purification offering, since its blood cleanses the sanctuary from the effects of sin and impurity, which is exactly what it does in verses 14 to 19. Roy Gane (Cult and Character, 2005) argues that on this day the offering purges the sanctuary of defilement already removed from the offerers during the year.

Tum'ah, uncleanness, impurity. It occurs about 36 times, most of them in Leviticus and Numbers. It names the ritual condition that results from childbirth, skin disease, discharges, and contact with the dead (Leviticus 12 to 15), which is not in itself sinful but must be kept away from the holy. Verse 16 pairs it with pesha, rebellion, and verse 19 cleanses the altar from it. Ezekiel later uses the word for the moral defilement that drove Israel into exile (Ezekiel 36:17, 25), which God promises to cleanse.

Anah, to be low, and in the Piel to humble or afflict. The verb is common (about 80 times in its main senses) and often means to oppress. With nefesh, soul or self, it forms the idiom of verses 29 and 31, ‘afflict yourselves’, which ancient Jewish interpretation took as fasting (compare Isaiah 58:3-5 and Psalm 35:13). The humbling is bodily and inward together: the people deny their appetites while the high priest makes atonement, joining their repentance to the rite.

Shabbaton, a solemn rest. It occurs 11 times, always in Exodus and Leviticus. In the phrase shabbat shabbaton, ‘a Sabbath of complete rest’ (verse 31), it forms a superlative like the holy of holies. The full phrase is used only for the weekly Sabbath (Exodus 31:15, Leviticus 23:3) and for this day (Leviticus 23:32), which is why Jewish tradition calls Yom Kippur the Sabbath of Sabbaths. Atonement is received in rest, not achieved by work.

Samakh, to lean, lay, or support. It occurs about 48 times, often for laying a hand on an offering (Leviticus 1:4, 3:2, 4:4) and for ordaining a successor (Numbers 27:18, 23). In verse 21 Aaron lays both hands on the live goat, and the verse spells out what the gesture means here: he confesses the people's sins and puts them on its head. Scholars debate whether the one-handed gesture in ordinary offerings means ownership, identification, or transfer, but here transfer is explicit.

christ:
The letter to the Hebrews reads Jesus' work directly through this chapter. It recalls that “only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood” (Hebrews 9:7), and then says that Christ “entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). The comparison runs point by point. Aaron needed a bull for his own sin first (verses 6, 11); Hebrews presents Jesus as a sinless priest who “does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 7:27). Aaron entered a tent made by hands; Christ entered “heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (Hebrews 9:24). Aaron repeated the rite every year, which Hebrews takes as a sign that it could not finish the work, since “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4); Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself” (Hebrews 9:26).

The bodies of the sin offerings burned outside the camp (verse 27) become, in Hebrews 13:11-12, a picture of Jesus, who “suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood”. The curtain that barred everyone but the high priest becomes, in Hebrews 10:19-20, the way opened for all “through the curtain of His body”, and the Gospels record that at Jesus' death “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). Paul calls Christ the hilastērion, the word the Greek Old Testament used for the mercy seat (Romans 3:25), and 1 John 2:2 calls him “the atoning sacrifice for our sins”.

The New Testament does not explicitly connect the live goat with Christ, but the church has seen in it a picture of sin carried away, which fits the language of Isaiah 53, where “the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” and he “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:6, 12), and John the Baptist's words, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). Early writers such as the Epistle of Barnabas and Justin Martyr read the two goats together as Christ suffering and Christ returning; the link is typological and should be taught as such. The day's promise, that the people “will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (verse 30), is what Christians confess God has done in Christ once and for all.
interpretation:
Jewish reflection on the day began within the Second Temple period. Ben Sira, writing around 180 BC, praises the high priest Simon son of Onias and describes him coming out from behind the curtain in glory (Sirach 50:5-21), a scene many readers, and later the Avodah poets, connect with the Day of Atonement, though some scholars think it describes the daily offering. Philo read the two goats and the fast allegorically and ethically, and Jubilees ties the date to the day Joseph's brothers deceived Jacob with a goat's blood (Jubilees 34:12-19). The Mishnah's tractate Yoma preserves the rite in detail, down to the high priest's confession over the goat and the people's response when they heard the divine name (m. Yoma 6:2), and it closes with Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah's teaching from verse 30 that the day atones for sins against God but not for wrongs against a neighbor until the neighbor is reconciled (m. Yoma 8:9). Leviticus Rabbah 20 and 21, on the portion Acharei Mot, reflects on the death of Aaron's sons and on the high priest's entrance.

Medieval Jewish commentators wrestled with Azazel. Rashi, following the Talmud (b. Yoma 67b), took it as a hard, rocky place. Abraham ibn Ezra hinted that the reader who counts thirty-three verses on will understand the secret, a count Nahmanides explained as reaching Leviticus 17:7, which forbids sacrifices to goat-demons; Nahmanides, drawing on Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, described the goat as a portion given at God's command to the power of desolation, not as worship of it. Maimonides taught that the goat atones for all transgressions for those who repent, and for lighter ones even without repentance (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 1:2). In the synagogue, Leviticus 16 is read on the morning of Yom Kippur, with Isaiah 57:14-58:14 as its prophetic reading, and the additional service recites the Avodah, a poetic retelling of the high priest's service; Atah Konanta, among the oldest, is associated with Yose ben Yose, and Ashkenazi congregations recite Amitz Koach.

Christian reading began with Hebrews. The Epistle of Barnabas (chapter 7) and Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 40) took the two goats as Christ in his suffering and in his return. Origen's Homilies on Leviticus read the chapter at length, and in the tenth homily he compared the released goat with Barabbas and the man who sent it away with Pilate. William Tyndale coined scapegoat for his translation of the Pentateuch in 1530, and the word passed into ordinary English. Christian lectionaries seldom read Leviticus 16 itself; the church has heard it chiefly through Hebrews 9 and 10, read in Holy Week and on Good Friday.

Modern scholarship was reshaped by Jacob Milgrom's Anchor Bible commentary (Leviticus 1-16, 1991) and his 1976 article comparing the sanctuary to the portrait in Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray, which records its owner's corruption. Mary Douglas (Leviticus as Literature, 1999) read the book's rituals as a coherent symbolic system, and Roy Gane (2005) and Jay Sklar (2005) refined the understanding of purification and ransom. René Girard's The Scapegoat (English translation 1986) used the English word for a theory of collective violence against innocent victims, though the Levitical goat is not a victim of a mob. In art, William Holman Hunt painted The Scapegoat on the shore of the Dead Sea in 1854 and finished it in London in 1856; the larger version hangs in the Lady Lever Art Gallery at Port Sunlight.
text:
English Bibles differ most visibly over Azazel. The King James Version and the BSB translate ‘scapegoat’ (verses 8, 10, 26), following the Septuagint's ‘the one sent away’ and the Vulgate's ‘the goat sent out’; the RSV, NRSV, ESV, and NIV keep the Hebrew name Azazel, usually with a note, because the parallel with ‘for the LORD’ in verse 8 suggests a proper name. In verse 1 the Masoretic Text says only that Aaron's sons died ‘when they drew near before the LORD’; the Septuagint adds that they offered strange fire, supplying the detail from 10:1. The shorter Hebrew is almost certainly original.

Other differences come from the Hebrew itself. In verse 10 the phrase literally ‘to make atonement upon it’ is rendered by the BSB as “to make atonement by sending it”, by others as ‘to make atonement over it’. In verse 18 the altar ‘before the LORD’ is identified by the Mishnah as the golden incense altar and by many modern scholars as the altar of burnt offering, and translations do not settle the question. In verse 21 the rare word itti, used only here, is rendered ‘appointed’, ‘ready’, or ‘fit’. In verse 30 the final clause can be divided ‘you will be clean from all your sins, before the LORD’ or ‘from all your sins before the LORD you will be clean’, the second being the basis of the Mishnah's teaching in m. Yoma 8:9. The verse numbering of Leviticus 16 is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: The holy God provides a way to remain among a sinful people: once a year the sanctuary is cleansed with blood and the people's confessed sins are carried away, a provision that Hebrews says Christ fulfilled once for all.

outline.t: Coming near to God is a gift with conditions; the death of Aaron's sons shows that God is not safe to approach on our own terms.
The high priest comes in humility, in plain linen, bringing an offering for his own sin before he represents anyone else.
God provides both the means and the order of atonement, choosing by lot the goat that dies and the goat that carries sin away.
Sin defiles more than the sinner; blood brought into God's presence cleanses the sanctuary, the tent, and the altar.
Confessed sin is laid on a substitute and carried away to a place from which it does not return.
Holiness and uncleanness are kept apart to the end, and those who handled the offerings wash before rejoining the camp.
The people receive atonement by humbling themselves and resting, not by working, and the provision is renewed every year.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats the ritual as magic, as if blood and goats worked mechanically; the chapter puts the rite inside God's command, the high priest's confession, and the people's humbling, and the rabbis and the church alike rejected any atonement without repentance. The second treats the ritual as primitive and irrelevant; the New Testament's most developed account of Christ's work, in Hebrews, is built on it. The third merges the two goats into one and loses the chapter's point: one goat's blood cleanses the sanctuary, the other goat removes the people's guilt. A fourth takes Azazel as a being who receives an offering; the text gives sacrifice only to the LORD, whatever Azazel means.

Teachers should also be careful with allegory. The church has seen Christ in both goats, which is fair as typology, but details such as the man who leads the goat or the scarlet thread in later tradition should not be pressed into doctrine. And they should avoid presenting the Jewish observance of Yom Kippur as empty or merely legal; the rabbinic tradition's insistence on repentance and reconciliation with one's neighbor (m. Yoma 8:9) is itself a searching word to Christian readers.
teach.pastoral: This chapter can speak deeply to people who carry guilt they cannot shake, and to those with scrupulous consciences who confess the same sins again and again without believing they are forgiven. The picture of sins carried to a land cut off, from which the goat does not return, is meant to assure. It may also press on those who have been harmed by others' sin and feel defiled by it; the chapter's distinction between impurity and sin, and its concern for cleansing the whole community, can help such people see that defilement suffered is not the same as guilt incurred. For those grieving a sudden death, the chapter's opening reference to Aaron's sons, spoken to a grieving father, should be handled gently: God's word to Aaron after loss is not an explanation of the loss but a way to come near.

hard.q: How could the blood of animals, or a goat sent into the desert, really deal with human guilt?
hard.a:
The question is old; the New Testament raises it itself, saying “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). The philosophical objection was sharpened by Immanuel Kant in Religion within the Bounds of Mere Reason (1793), who argued that guilt is the most personal of all debts and cannot be transferred to another, however willing, the way a money debt can. Faustus Socinus (On Jesus Christ the Savior, completed 1578 and published 1594) had already argued that punishment of an innocent substitute is unjust. On this view the whole idea of sin laid on a goat, or on anyone else, is a primitive confusion of moral guilt with physical dirt, and modern readers often see the ritual as a kind of magic.

The responses come from Jewish and Christian readers alike. Jewish interpreters have long answered that the rite never worked apart from repentance: the people fasted and humbled themselves, the Mishnah teaches that repentance atones together with the day (m. Yoma 8:8), and wrongs against a neighbor require making things right with the neighbor first (m. Yoma 8:9). Maimonides taught that the goat atones for grave sins only for those who repent. Christian interpreters generally agree that the animals had no power in themselves: Leviticus 17:11 says the blood atones because God has given it for that purpose. Scholars such as Jacob Milgrom have stressed that the rite is about cleansing the sanctuary so that God can remain present, not about bribing or appeasing him. On the Christian reading, the Day of Atonement was God's real provision for Israel's life with him in its time, and also a picture pointing ahead to a sacrifice that could do fully what the annual rite could only signify; Christian theologians answering Kant argue that Christ's self-offering is not a transfer between strangers but the act of the one who is both God and the representative head of his people. Many Jewish readers, by contrast, see the rite as complete in its own terms, and after the temple's destruction in AD 70 they kept the day through prayer, fasting, and repentance. The disagreement between these readings is real, and a reader can see both taking seriously the chapter's claim that God himself provides the way back.

hard.q: Who or what is Azazel, and was the goat sent to a demon?
hard.a:
The strongest form of the question is critical. The phrase ‘one for the LORD and one for Azazel’ (verse 8) sets the two names in parallel, which suggests that Azazel is a personal being, and the book of 1 Enoch, from the third or second century BC, names Azazel as a fallen angel bound in the desert (1 Enoch 8:1, 10:4-8). Leviticus 17:7 forbids Israel to sacrifice to goat-demons (se'irim), which shows such beliefs were real. Many modern scholars, Jacob Milgrom among them, hold that Azazel was originally a wilderness demon, and some critics conclude that the rite preserves a pre-Israelite offering to a desert spirit only lightly reshaped by monotheism.

The responses take several forms. The Septuagint and the Vulgate read the word as a description of the goat, the one sent away, and Tyndale's scapegoat follows them. The Talmud (b. Yoma 67b) and Rashi took Azazel as the name of a rugged place, and G. R. Driver argued from Arabic for a word meaning rough ground. Others read it as an abstract term, ‘for complete removal’. Among medieval Jewish readers, Nahmanides accepted a link with the power of desolation but insisted that the goat is sent at God's command and is not worship. Milgrom himself argued that whatever Azazel once meant, Leviticus has stripped it of power: the goat is not slaughtered, nothing is offered to Azazel, and the lots are cast before the LORD. On every reading, the chapter's theology is clear. Only the LORD receives sacrifice, and the goat's task is to carry Israel's confessed sins away from the camp to the place of desolation where they belong. Which reading of the word is right remains an open question, and faithful interpreters hold each of them.

observe: What must Aaron do before he can make atonement for the people, and what does he wear when he enters the Most Holy Place?
List the things for which atonement is made in this chapter. Which are places and which are people?
What does Aaron do with the live goat, and what does the goat carry into the wilderness?
interpret: Why do you think the chapter needs two goats, one killed and one sent away? What does each show about how God deals with sin?
Why would the sanctuary itself need cleansing if it was the people who sinned?
How does Hebrews 9 use this chapter, and what does it say is the same and what is different in Christ's work?
apply: The chapter treats sin as something that stains a whole community and its place of worship, not only the individual. Where do you see the effects of wrongdoing spreading beyond the person who did it?
Aaron had to make atonement for himself before he could do it for anyone else. What does that say about the people we trust to lead us spiritually, and about ourselves when we try to help others?
The live goat carried confessed sins far away. What would it mean for you to believe that a wrong you have confessed is truly gone?
